$comment: Regimes: states of the world that a FIXTURE fixes before a call, not states that the
call's arguments choose. A predicate over a regime never varies inside a single test, so
condition coverage cannot reach it by varying inputs, and a mutant on it dies in whichever
regime the fixtures happen to agree on.
Each entry names the call a test makes to put the world in that regime. Its ABSENCE is the
other regime, which is why the entry names only the ON side.
Adding a regime here multiplies the lattice and will lower the coverage ratio until the new
cells are answered. That is the intended behaviour of a completeness measure.

regimes.name: bridge
regimes.why: decides whether the fee is anchored to one hop or charged on every hop

regimes.name: renounced
regimes.why: the terminal state the system is designed to reach; nothing can answer a hazard after it

regimes.name: paused
regimes.why: the only reversible refusal, and the one that dies with the control plane

regimes.name: hook
regimes.why: admits a third party into the execution path of a swap

regimes.name: v4
regimes.why: a singleton venue whose pools are derived rather than deployed

regimes.name: permit2
regimes.why: delegated approval moves the authority for pulling funds outside this system

regimes.name: native
regimes.why: the wrap/unwrap bijection is the only place value changes representation

regimes.name: operator
regimes.why: a seat that outlives renunciation, so what it can still do is bounded by nothing else

shapes.name: multi-hop
shapes.why: composition is where properties that hold per hop stop holding per route

oracles.name: cross-producer
oracles.why: the expected value comes from a producer independent of the one under test, rather than from a literal, the code's own output, or a helper that reuses production arithmetic
